Q: How redundancy effects Data Compression? A:

There may be some confusion of terminology here. Database practioners and the data compression theorists use the word "redundancy" to mean different things. Because you refer to SQL, I am guessing that you are thinking of normalization as a way of reducing redundancy in a set of relations in a database. In data compression, they are looking at "redundancy" as trends in how often a symbol is repeated in a text. For example, a text consisting of only a single symbol compress much more effectively than one consisting a a random mix of characters. In the first case, you could just encode your text as something like "write 10 thousand letters A". If the second case, no such opportunity exists.

The modern concept of redundancy for data compression looks at the degree to which "the next symbol" in a text is predictable. This idea was rigorously described by Claude Shannon in his famous 1948 paper “A Mathematical Theory of Communication”. But if you're just getting started, I recommend looking at "The Data Compression Book" by Mark Nelson which gives a accessible explanation of the fundamental concepts. And, if you're serious about computer science, by all means learn more about Mr. Shannon.

Finally, I add that I've posted a web article about entropy and data compression. The term "information entropy" is kind of the opposite of redundancy. You can read it at What entropy tells us about data compression.

Q: Using PowerShell and wkhtmltopdf to output to PDF A:

tl;dr

Building on your own answer:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse -File -LiteralPath test_input | 
  ForEach-Object { 
    & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" -O landscape --enable-local-file-access $_.FullName "test_output\$($_.BaseName).pdf" 
  }

Note:

  • For conceptual clarity the above uses the ForEach-Object cmdlet's full name in lieu of %, which is one of its built-in aliases.

  • It is only the fact that you've specified the target executable in quotes that syntactically requires its invocation via &, the call operator; without quotes (and in the absence of variable references), & is optional - see this answer for more.
    In other words: & "wkhtmltopdf.exe" could be replaced with just wkhtmltopdf.exe here.

  • -attributes !directory has been replaced with -File to request file-only output, which is more concise and conceptually direct.

  • Since the input path, test_input, contains no wildcard characters, I'm assuming it is to be treated literally (verbatim), in which case the robust choice is to use -LiteralPath rather than -Path, as literal input paths that happen to contain [ / ] would otherwise be misinterpreted; see this answer for more informcation.

Detailed explanation:

I suspect the problem is the \\$_.pdf part

Indeed:

  • Incidentally, using \\ in lieu of \ is unnecessary, but benign: In PowerShell itself, \ has no special meaning and therefore doesn't require escaping - see the bottom section of this answer for more information.
    However, using verbatim \\ as a path separator is generally quietly tolerated.

  • Crucially, however, $_ contains the full path of the input file at hand, due to the preceding % { $_.fullname } pipeline segment, whereas your intent was for $_ refer to the base name, i.e. the mere file name of the input without its extension.

I've tried a bunch of different properties on the $_ object, and length is the only one that has substituted a value, so I have no idea what's going on.

  • % { $_.fullname } (% being a built-in alias of the built-in ForEach-Object cmdlet) emits the full path of each input file as a string, i.e. an instance of [string], whose only (.NET type-native) property is .Length

  • In PowerShell - by default - any attempt to reference a nonexistent property quietly results in $null being returned.

    • In the context of string interpolation, i.e. inside an expandable (interpolating) string (double-quoted, i.e. "..."), $null simply becomes the empty string, i.e. doesn't contribute any characters to the resulting string, which explains the outcome of your attempt to use an (imagined) .namestring property.

    • Via Set-StrictMode -Version 2 or above, you could instruct PowerShell to report errors in response to attempts to access nonexistent properties, but that comes with pitfalls - see this answer.

Therefore:

  • Do not use % { $_.fullname }, as it prevents you from (easily) deriving the base file name from each input file in subsequent pipeline segments.

  • Using the input file objects emitted by Get-ChildItem - which are of type System.IO.FileInfo - as-is, allows you to conveniently reference the base file name as $_.BaseName

    • Inside "..." - as shown in your own answer - referencing $_.BaseName requires enclosure in $(...), for syntactic reasons explained in this answer.

Q: How can I skip the rest of tests in the class if one has failed? A:

Or quite simply instead of calling py.test from cmd (or tox or wherever), just call:

py.test --maxfail=1

see here for more switches: https://pytest.org/latest/usage.html

Q: Understanding "I/O depth" aka "queues" (e.g. in the fio "flexible I/O tester") A:

The most simple way to have IO queue depth > 1 is to have multiple processes or threads all doing I/O at once, like a web server that's serving 50 different requests at the same time, each one opening and reading a different file. (In reality you'd often have some of them reading the same file so those being satisfied from cache, but that's just extra CPU load so you ignore that for I/O testing.)

Or for writes, large queue depth happens naturally: one big sequential I/O has to be broken up into blocks of the max size the hardware interface (e.g. SATA or NVMe) can handle. A write system-call will return when the data has been copied to kernel buffers, before it actually makes it to hardware. If the SATA link is faster than the physical disk (which is normal), the kernel can keep submitting I/Os to the hard drive until the SATA queue is full (typically 32). Separate small write system-calls can also easily lead to higher queue depth, especially on rotational media with high seek times, since again the kernel will buffer output.

A single thread can also generate multiple read I/Os in parallel with aio stuff, and might do so after e.g. receiving HTTP requests for multiple files in a single HTTP connection, processing further requests while sending the reply to the first GET request.

readv is about scattering one contiguous read to separate memory locations (e.g. a few different arrays that were packed head-to-tail in a file), not generating multiple small I/Os. Similarly writev is about gathering data from memory into one contiguous write. You might use it if you had a bunch of small structs, and want to grab just part of each struct for some file format. Or an array of char-pointers or something, to concatenate all those strings into a file with a single system-call.

Q: How do web platforms like Twitter, Instagram or Facebook allow other web sites to embed their content? A:

Really all you have to do is create a block of code that has what you want on it (a link or something, perhaps) and then post that block of code somewhere on your website. Then people can just copy/paste the code over.
